tools.name: get_workspace
tools.title: Read the workspace
tools.description: Every form in the editor's workspace, the one being edited first. Each has its index (its place in this list, which the other tools take), its settings as names and values, its grid's angle in degrees, its colour, where it stands in microbricks, the box its bricks fill (`box_in_grid`: low and high corners and size within its own grid; `box_in_world`: the same box's extent and centre in the world, which differs when the grid is at an angle), how many bricks it was fitted with, and its discrepancy: the volume where the bricks and the true form disagree, as a percentage of the form's volume. A form's `points` are measured from where it stands (`place`), so a point's position in its grid is the point plus `place`. Call this first, and again whenever the player may have changed something by hand.

tools.name: add_form
tools.title: Add a form
tools.description:
Add a form to the workspace. It becomes the form being edited (index 0) and is set down beside the forms already there unless `place` is given. The camera flies to face it. Returns the workspace afresh. All lengths are in microbricks (a fifth of a stud); a point or a size may end in a half.

Settings (give `form` and whichever others are not to keep their usual values; a form given no `points` is set down where the editor would start one):
- form: one of `arch round`, `arch pointed`, `arch triangular`, `arch elliptical`, `arch parabolic`, `arch catenary`, `circle`, `spline`, `bezier`, `sphere`, `revolve`, `pyramid`, `cube`, `tree` (a tree, a bush or a flower), `furniture` (a bookcase, cupboards, tables, seating, lamps, a bed, plants in pots, pictures), `maze`, `imported` (a mesh from a file the player has opened: see `import`).
- points: a list of [x, y, z]. An arch: its two feet. A circle, sphere or pyramid: its centre. A cube: its middle. A tree: the foot of its trunk or stem. Furniture: the middle of the box it fills. A maze: the middle of its floor. A spline or bezier: the points it is drawn through or pulled towards, in order. A revolve: its profile, from the top down, as points in the plane y = the first point's, x being the distance out from the upright axis through x = 0.
- radius: of a circle or sphere; half the width of a pyramid's base; half the side of a cube; how far a tree reaches to each side (a pine's longest boughs, a palm's fronds, an oak's crown, a bush's half width; for a sunflower or tulip half the width of its head or cup).
- rise: an arch's height above its feet, a pyramid's height or a plant's, or `natural` for the height the shape gives.
- tree: which plant a `tree` form is, as text `kind,seed,fullness,count,bend,extras`, of which only the kind is needed. Kinds: `pine` (a spruce, the Christmas tree), `palm` (a coconut palm), `oak`, `beech`, `boxwood` (a dense rounded bush), `hedge` (boxwood clipped to a wall), `hydrangea`, `peony`, `sunflower`, `tulip`, `petunia`, `reeds`, `grass`, `birch`, `willow` (weeping), `datepalm`, `scotspine`, `cypress`, `yucca`, `daisy`, `daffodil`, `bed` (mixed flowers), `cherry` (a Japanese cherry in blossom), `flower` (a single flower head with no plant under it: see `bloom`) (`rose` is read as `peony`). seed: any whole number, each a different plant of the kind. fullness, 0 to 100: foliage, petals or leaves. count: a pine's tiers of boughs (4 to 40), a palm's fronds (5 to 40), the limbs an oak's (2 to 7) or beech's (3 to 9) trunk divides into, a boxwood's stems (2 to 12), the plants along a hedge (1 to 40), a hydrangea's flower heads (1 to 24), the stems in a clump of peonies (1 to 9), the flowers in a clump of sunflowers or tulips (1 to 12), a petunia's flowers (3 to 80), a stand of reeds' stems (1 to 120). bend, 0 to 100: how far a pine's boughs droop, a palm's trunk leans, an oak's or beech's limbs are crooked, a boxwood's, hedge's or hydrangea's outline is uneven, how open a peony's bloom is (0 a round bud, 100 full blown) or a tulip's cup, a sunflower's head nods, petunias trail, reeds sway. extras, 1 or 0: a pine's star and baubles, a palm's coconuts, an oak or beech bare of leaves (with twigs), berries on a boxwood or hedge, feathery plumes on reeds in place of a bulrush's brown heads. `oak,3` is the third oak; `beech,1,65,6,30,1` a bare beech; `peony,2,60,5,0` five peonies in bud. A hedge, a stand of reeds or a patch of `grass` lies along a line: give two or more `points` and it follows the smooth curve through them (`closed` true makes a ring of a hedge and a filled outline of grass), and `radius` is how far it reaches to each side of the line, which changing leaves its length alone; with one point it is straight along x, `stretch` `[n, 1, 1]` times as long as `radius`, three times if not given. Grass's `rise` is the length of its blades (8 if not given) and its `radius` 20. Its ground is shaped by add_pull_point, each a touch of a brush: `at` is where and `pulled_by` is `[range, flatten, amount]`, flatten 0 to push the ground up by `amount` (down if negative, never below the floor) over a smooth hill `range` wide, or 16 to flatten it to the height `amount`; add 32 to either (32 or 48) for a touch with a sharp edge, which does all it does out to a narrow band at the edge of its range and falls away there, a table or a pit with sides steep enough to be cliffs; at most 240 touches, applied in order. The ground may be dug below the lawn's level, and grass's count is how far below the lawn water stands (0 to 40, 3 if not given, 0 for none): a hollow deeper than that is a pond, with sand at its bank, stones on its bed, water to the level, and reeds round it as thickly as `depth` less 1 says (0 to 10). `protrude` true runs a hedge, reeds or grass straight between its points with a sharp corner at each. `fill` true on grass freezes its pond: the water is written as ice, with collision on. `tube` true on grass gives it raised ponds: a hollow on raised ground holds a pond of its own, each at the height its own rim gives it, and a stream runs downhill from it to the nearest water that stands lower, going over any cliff on the way as a waterfall with white water where it lands (the levels follow the sculpted ground; none is typed). The eighth number of grass's `tree` is how readily steep ground is a cliff, 0 to 3 (0, for none, if not given): past a first steepness the ground is bare soil and past a second it is rock in ledges, at 52 and 68 degrees for 1, 45 and 61 for 2, 36 and 53 for 3. `tube` true on any other plant writes its greenery (leaves, needles, fronds, petals, berries) with collision off in the game and keeps its wood solid. For the new kinds: count is a birch's, willow's or Scots pine's main limbs (3 to 9), a date palm's fronds (8 to 60), a yucca's blades (8 to 80), the flowers in a clump of daisies or daffodils (1 to 20) or in a bed (2 to 40); a cherry's main limbs (3 to 9); a pine is dressed as a Christmas tree by its extras (1 for a star on top) and four more numbers after the trunk width: baubles (0 to 100, how many), tinsel (1 or 0), lights (0 none, 1 a string of lights, 2 candles; 40 at most) and whether the lights shine in the game (1, each with a point light on it, or 0 for glowing bricks alone), and a fifth for how far out the tinsel hangs (40 to 110, a percentage of the way from the stem to the ends of the boughs, 80 if not given), so `pine,1,60,15,50,1,100,60,1,1,1,80` is a fully dressed one; in the game its baubles, tinsel and star are the metallic material and its lights the glowing one; a seventh number is a tree's trunk width as a percentage of what is usual for its kind (50 to 200, 100 if not given; pine, palm, date palm, oak, beech, birch, willow, Scots pine, cypress and cherry, and nothing to a bush or flower), with its limbs thicker or thinner to match; extras is bare for a birch, willow, Scots pine or cherry (`closed` true on a cherry scatters fallen petals under it), dates for a date palm, the flower stalk for a yucca. Grass's extras, 1 or 0: 1 makes its blades solid in the game, 0 (the usual) writes them with collision off so a player walks through them onto the soil. A plant given no radius or rise is its usual size (a pine 140 tall, a palm 120, an oak 110, a beech 140, a boxwood 40, a hedge 36, a hydrangea 46, a peony 56, a sunflower 90, a tulip 64, petunias 20, reeds 84), is thousands to tens of thousands of bricks, and takes up to a second to build; it comes in its own colours (mode `pattern`, eight colours: trunk or stem, leaves, leaves in shade, new growth, limbs, then petals or the top of a pine's boughs, a second petal colour or throats or berries or brown heads or the extras, and the heart of a flower) unless `colour` is given. A plant has no thick, depth, fill, mirror or pulls.
- hedge: `true` builds an arch as clipped hedge in place of plain brick, `false` (the usual) as brick. The hedge is the `tree` kind `hedge` grown over the arch's own band, so the `tree` setting says how it is grown: `hedge,seed,fullness,count,bend,extras`, fullness its density, bend its looseness, extras 1 for berries; its count is unused. `thick` and `depth` are the band's as for a plain arch, each 6 at the least for a hedge (a thinner arch is built 6). The opening keeps the plain arch's shape to within one microbrick a side. It comes in a hedge's eight colours with the mode `pattern`, is some thousands of bricks, and one too large for single microbricks is built at a larger brick size. Other forms take no notice of it; a maze's hedges are its own `maze` setting.
- bloom: which flower a `tree` of the kind `flower` is and how it lies, as text `flower,tilt,turn,stem,fallen`, of which only the flower is needed. Flowers: `rose` (a high-centred double rose), `waterlily`, `gerbera` (a large daisy). tilt, 0 to 90: how far the bloom is tipped over from facing straight up, in degrees; 90 lies on its side. turn, 0 to 359: which way round it is tipped, in degrees about the upright, 0 towards +x. stem, 1 or 0: a short length of stem behind it. fallen, 1 or 0: a few loose petals on the floor beside it. The bloom is grown along the slant and set down on whatever part of it is lowest, so it is never below the floor of its point. For this kind the `tree` setting's fullness is how many petals, its bend how open the bloom is (0 a closed bud, 100 full blown), its extras the sepals under it, and its count is unused; `radius` is half the full-blown bloom's width (24 if not given) and `rise` how deep the bloom is (28). `"tree": "flower"` alone is a red rose 60% open facing up; with `"bloom": "rose,60,45,1,1"` it lies tipped over on its stem with petals beside it; `"tree": "flower,1,60,1,0"` is a bud. Its colour numbers are stem, sepals, a petal's throat, a petal's lip, the swelling under the bloom, two tones of petal, and the stamens or disc.
- maze: which maze a `maze` form is, as text `kind,rings,divisions,grow,seed,entrance,floor,solution,hedge`, of which only the kind is needed. kind: `theta` (rings of corridors about a round room, the walls arcs and spokes) or `grid` (square cells about a square room). rings, 2 to 40: how many rings, the room in the middle counted as the first; a grid has that many cells from its middle to its edge. divisions, 1 to 64: how many cells the first ring of a theta maze is cut into. grow, 0 to 8: how the number of cells grows outwards in a theta maze, 0 doubling it wherever the cells would otherwise be over twice as wide as a corridor, and any other number doubling it every that many rings (2 is what the old brickmaze generator did). seed: any whole number, each a different maze. entrance: where on the rim the way in is, in degrees round from the x axis. floor, 0 to 8: how thick a floor under the whole maze is, 0 for none. solution, 1 or 0: 1 lays a strip a microbrick high along the ground from the way in to the room. hedge, 1 or 0: 1 makes the walls hedge, grown as a `tree` form's hedge is, whose `tree` settings give its fullness, bend and extras (berries). The form's `radius` is from the middle to the middle of the outside wall, so a corridor with one wall is `radius` divided by `rings` (by `rings` less a half for a grid) and must leave 3 or more between walls; `thick` is the walls' thickness, a whole number (6 at least for hedge); `rise` their height (12 at least for hedge). Left out, they are 120, 4 and 30. `mosaic` wraps a pattern along every wall and not through the maze from above: `bricks` in level courses that bend round the rings, `cobblestone`, `planks` or `medallions`; a `rug` and `stones` are not laid on a maze, and bevel and border do nothing to one. A pattern colours the walls and never moves them. Every maze has one way in and one way to the room, with no loops, and every cell can be reached. It comes in its own colours (mode `pattern`) unless `colour` is given: with plain walls three, the floor, the walls and the way through; with a pattern or hedge eight, the first being the floor and the mortar or stems and the last the way through. `theta,8,4,0,3` is the third maze of 8 rings; `grid,5,4,0,1,90,1,1,0` a grid with a floor and its way through marked, entered from +y. A maze is refused, with what to change, if its corridors are too narrow, its walls over 40,000 microbricks long in all, or its hedge too much to build; plain it is hundreds to a few thousand bricks, patterned or hedge tens of thousands. A maze has no depth, fill, tube, mirror or pulls.
- thick: the thickness of a band, a tube or a hollow form's wall.
- A cube is a box of whole bricks, for a floor, a wall, a slab or a room: `radius` is half its side and `stretch` scales that along x, y and z, so a floor 40 by 30 and 2 deep is radius 20 with stretch [1, 0.75, 0.05]. Each length is rounded to a whole microbrick, 1 at least. `fill` true is solid; false is hollow with walls `thick` on every side, or a frame where the box is too short to have a hollow inside. `mosaic` and `stones` are laid through its shortest length, so they show on its largest face. `depth`, `tube` and `plane` do nothing to it.
- furniture: which piece a `furniture` form is, as text `kind,seed,board,shelves,spacing,bay,plinth,back,moulding,books,style,count,choice,second,extra,shine`, of which only the kind is needed. Kinds: `bookcase`; `cupboard`, `drawers` (a chest of them), `sideboard`, `kitchen` (a cabinet under a worktop); `dining`, `coffee`, `side` (tables), `desk`; `chair`, `armchair`, `stool`, `bench`, `sofa`; `tablelamp`, `floorlamp`, `pendant`, `chandelier`, `sconce`, `candlestick`; `bed`; `potted` (a plant in a pot), `basket` (a hanging one), `windowbox`, `trellis` (in a planter, with a climber); `painting`, `portrait` (framed, to hang on a wall). Every piece fills the box a cube of the same `radius` and `stretch` would fill and is laid out afresh at any size; its one point is the middle of that box, its front is on the low y side (use `turned` to face it another way), and a pendant or chandelier hangs from the top of its box while a sconce, a trellis and a picture are against its high y side. Given no radius or stretch a piece is its usual size (a dining table 44 by 24 by 19, a chair 11 by 11 by 23, a cupboard 30 by 14 by 50, a sofa 50 by 21 by 21, a bookcase 36 by 10 by 60), and given no points it stands on the floor. seed: any whole number. style: `modern`, `farmhouse`, `classical`, `rustic`, `industrial`, or `random` (the seed picks). Pieces with the same style and the same seed are a set, with the same legs, weight and woods: to furnish a room give every piece the same two. count, 0 for as many as the size has room for: a cupboard's doors, a chest's or desk's drawers, a kitchen's units, a sofa's seats, a pot's height in tenths of the whole, the microbricks between a trellis's slats. choice, 0 for the style's: table legs (1 square, 2 tapered, 3 turned, 4 trestle, 5 pedestal), a chair's or bench's back (1 slats, 2 ladder, 3 panel, 4 spindles), a stool's seat (1 square, 2 round), a sofa's arms (1 square, 2 rolled), cupboard handles (1 knobs, 2 bars, 3 none), a lamp's shade (1 drum, 2 cone, 3 globe), a headboard (1 panel, 2 slats, 3 rails), a pot (1 terracotta, 2 glazed, 3 square planter, 4 tall planter), a lattice (1 square, 2 diamond, 3 arched), a painting's subject (1 sunset, 2 landscape, 3 abstract), what a portrait's sitter wears (1 nothing, 2 glasses, 3 a hat, 4 a beard). second, 0 for the style's or the seed's: a table top (1 rectangular, 2 round), a seat (1 bare, 2 cushion), what a sofa stands on (1 legs, 2 a skirt) or a cupboard (1 a plinth, 2 feet), a chandelier's arms (1 two, 2 four, 3 eight candles), a candlestick (1 one candle, 2 three), pillows (1 or 2), the plant in a pot (1 yucca, 2 boxwood, 3 hydrangea, 4 peonies, 5 tulips, 6 daffodils, 7 daisies, 8 petunias, 9 cypress, 10 palm, 11 cherry), a climber (1 ivy, 2 clematis, 3 rose, 4 wisteria, 5 none). extra, 1 or 0: stretchers on a dining table, a shelf under a coffee table, a side table's drawer, a desk's second pedestal, a chair's arms, a bench's back, a drawer row under a cupboard's doors, two small top drawers on a chest, drawers in a sideboard's middle, a drawer over each kitchen door, a footboard, a picture's mount, and for a plant in a pot whether its leaves are walked through in the game. shine, 1 or 0: whether a lamp's bulb or flames carry a real light in the game as well as glowing (one to a lamp, one to each candle, eight at most). A bookcase reads only seed and the eight values after it: board, how thick its boards are (1 to 8); shelves, how many between bottom and top, or 0 for as many as fit at `spacing`, the clear height between shelves (3 to 200); bay, the widest an opening may be before an upright divides it (4 to 400, 0 for none); plinth (0 to 20); back, 1 or 0, a back panel; moulding, 1 or 0, a cornice and skirting; books, 0 to 100, how full its shelves are. The other kinds read none of those, but a trellis reads books as how much of it its climber covers. `chair,4,2,0,11,34,3,1,1,85,farmhouse` is the fourth farmhouse chair, and `dining,4,2,0,11,34,3,1,1,85,farmhouse` the table that goes with it. Furniture is exact (no discrepancy), a few dozen to a few hundred bricks, and builds at once; a plant in a pot is the exception, its plant being fitted as plants are: hundreds to a few thousand bricks and a few tenths of a second. A piece comes in its style's own colours (mode `pattern`: wood, a second wood or paint, metal, upholstery, a second cloth, light, linen, a top; a bookcase its wood, its back and six for its books; a plant in a pot the pot, its rim, soil, stems, two greens and two flower colours; a picture its frame, liner, mount and up to twenty-six of its subject's) unless `colour` is given. `thick`, `depth`, `fill`, `tube`, `rise`, `mirror`, `pulls`, `grain`, `mosaic` and `stones` do nothing to it, and it is joined to other forms by cutting alone.
- depth: how deep a flat band is, a whole number.
- fill: true for a solid sphere, pyramid, revolve or cube, or to fill the area a curve encloses; false for a shell, or a band along the curve.
- tube: true builds a curve as a round tube (a circle then becomes a torus); false as a flat band.
- closed: true joins a spline's last point to its first.
- plane: the axis a circle faces along, 0 (x), 1 (y) or 2 (z, lying flat).
- stretch: [x, y, z] factors; 2 makes the form twice as long that way.
- cut: [low, high] keeps the part of a sphere between two heights measured from its centre (a dome is [0, "inf"]); `none` keeps it whole.
- weights: one number for each point of a bezier; higher draws the curve closer to that point.
- mirror: [x, y, z] of true or false; makes the form its own mirror image along that axis.
- flip: [x, y, z] of true or false; mirrors the finished form along that axis.
- turned: a quarter-turn pose within the brick grid, 0 to 23 (16 is upright).
- pulls: points added to pull the form out of shape, as text `x,y,z > dx,dy,dz; ...`: where each takes hold, then how far it moves. pull_reach: how far from each the form goes with it.
- on_grid: the number of the grid the form is on (0 is the world's). Forms sharing a number turn and move together.
- grid_degrees: [about x, about y, about z], the grid's angle in degrees, turned about x first, then y, then z. Any angle is allowed: the bricks stay as smooth as on a level grid. Give a form its own on_grid number before turning it, or every form on that grid is drawn at the angle of the last one set.
- grid_at: [x, y, z], where the grid's origin stands in the world.
- stones: [size, gap, uneven, seed] lays a flat band (or a filled outline) as a path of separate stepping stones in place of solid brick: `size` is about how far apart the stones' middles are, `gap` the space between stones, `uneven` 0 to 1 how much they differ, and `seed` any whole number, each a different scattering. `none` for solid brick. The band's `thick` is the path's width. Colour it with mode `pattern`, which gives each stone one of the colours; with no `colour` it comes in stone colours.
- mosaic: [style, size, bevel, border, seed] or [style, size, bevel, border, seed, mortar, stagger, upright, uneven_along, uneven_across] or the same with `0, depth` after it lays a flat form as a pattern of coloured tiles a microbrick across, square or cut diagonally into two triangles. `style` is one of `medallions` (ringed figures repeated over the floor), `rug` (a Persian carpet: nested borders, a lobed medallion with pendants, corner pieces, scrolling stems with flowers; it wants a rectangle 100 or more across to show its detail), both mirror-symmetric and set out from the middle of the floor; `planks` (a floor of boards); `bricks` (courses of bricks, every one a rectangle); or `cobblestone` (stones of any shape fitted together). `size` is how large the boards, bricks or cobbles are (2 is usual, 1 to 8); `border` how many microbricks of plain border; `seed` any whole number, each a different pattern. For bricks and cobblestone: `mortar` is 1 for a microbrick of mortar between pieces and 0 for none; the two `uneven` values, 0 to 100, are how unlike one another the pieces are along the courses and across them. For bricks alone: `bevel` is 1 to slope the top microbrick of every brick down to its edge (the form must be 2 or more deep) and 0 for flat, which it must be for every other style; `depth`, the twelfth value after a 0 in the eleventh place, is 1 to groove planks of size 3 or more (each row of boards one microbrick proud of the next) or to lay cobblestone's mortar one microbrick below its stones, in a form 2 or more deep, and 0 for flat; `stagger` is how far each course is moved along from the one before, in hundredths of a brick (50 is the usual bond, 0 stacks them, -1 moves each course by its own amount), and `upright` is 1 for courses running up the floor and 0 for across. Left out, the last five are 1, -1, 0, 0 and 0; give cobblestone about 60 and 60, since cobbles all alike are a grid of squares. `none` for no mosaic. A pattern is laid through a flat form, on the flat faces of a form that is not flat all over, and on the sides of a box; use it with `fill` true on a circle, closed curve or cube, and colour mode `pattern`: the first colour is the ground or the mortar and the rest are shared among the pattern's parts, up to eight. A form has `mosaic` or `stones`, not both.
- blend: joins the form to the forms it stands in, on the same grid: `0` for a plain union with a sharp crease, up to `6` for a fillet reaching that many microbricks along each form, or `none` for a form that stands apart. Give it together with a `place` that puts the form partly inside another. Forms are otherwise never fitted as one: two forms that overlap without `blend` are sent to the game with bricks missing. Where joined forms meet, the bricks are fitted afresh as one smooth solid, and elsewhere each form keeps its own. A joined form must stand a whole number of microbricks from the form it joins along every axis, so one given a `place` half a microbrick off is moved by that half, and the workspace returned says where it stands. (Two joined forms of one `grain` above 1 are moved to stand whole bricks of that size apart, and are then joined in bricks of that size.) It does nothing to a form laid as a pattern or to a plant, which are joined by cutting alone.
- carve: `true` takes a joined form away from the forms it is joined to, where `false` (the usual) adds it: a window through a wall, a hole through a sphere. It needs `blend` as well, which is then how far the rim of the hole is rounded, and a `place` that puts the form in what it is to cut. None of the form's own bricks are built, and it is listed with the bricks it would have.
- import: which mesh an `imported` form is built from and how, as text `name,up,fitter,loose,colours`, of which only the name is needed. name: one of the names list_meshes gives, which are the files in the editor's imports folder. No other file can be named: a mesh gets there by the player opening it in the editor (typing its path in the panel, or dropping the file on the window). up: which of the file's axes points up, `y` (the usual for .glb and .obj files), `z` or `x`. fitter: `smoothed` (ramps and corner pieces lying in the mesh's faces, the usual) or `blocks` (cubes only). loose: pieces of the build that touch no other piece and are smaller than this many microbricks are left out, 0 to 200, 0 (the usual) for none. colours: how many colours the mesh's own are reduced to, 0 to 32, 12 if not given; 0 leaves them out, and the form is then coloured by `colour`. For an imported form `radius` is half the length of the mesh's longest side (24 if not given), `points` is the middle of its box, `fill` true (the usual) fills its inside and false leaves a shell `thick` through, and `simplify` above 0 lets a stretched piece stand further from the mesh for each brick it saves. A mesh of many triangles at a large size takes seconds to fit, and `grain` 0 fits it at several sizes.
- grain: brick size, 0 for automatic or 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8; budget: the most bricks automatic may use; simplify: 0 to 1.5, higher for fewer bricks on flat outlines; max_ext: the longest edge a brick may have.

settings.description: Names and values as described above. `form` is required.

colour.description: How the form is coloured. Each brick is one colour.

mode.description: One colour, a gradual blend from the first colour to the last, stripes of each in turn, or `pattern`: each brick the colour its pattern gives it (the tiles of a mosaic, the stones of a path, the parts of a tree, the wood and books of a bookcase), the first colour being the ground and the rest shared among the pattern's parts.

colours.description: One to four colours as #rrggbb, or up to 32 for a pattern, a tree or furniture. A pattern has eight numbered parts at most and shares them among the colours given, so more than eight are of use only to a form with more parts.

runs_along.description: The direction a blend or stripes run in.

stripe_width.description: How wide each stripe is, in microbricks.

place.description: Where the form stands within its grid, [x, y, z] in microbricks; a value may end in a half.

tools.name: update_form
tools.title: Change a form
tools.description: Change one form: any of its settings (the names and values add_form describes), its colour, or where it stands. Only what is given changes. Nothing changes if any part of the request cannot be built, and the reason is returned. Returns the workspace afresh, with the form's new brick count and discrepancy, so the effect of a change can be checked and corrected. The player can take the change back with Ctrl+Z.

index.description: The form's place in the list get_workspace gives.

settings.description: The settings to change, as names and values.

colour.description: The parts of the colouring to change.

place.description: Where the form stands within its grid, [x, y, z] in microbricks.

tools.name: remove_form
tools.title: Remove a form
tools.description: Take one form out of the workspace. The last form cannot be removed. Returns the workspace afresh: the forms after the one removed each move up one place.

index.description: The form's place in the list get_workspace gives.

tools.name: select_form
tools.title: Edit a form
tools.description: Make one form the form being edited, so that the player sees its dots, arrows and rings and its settings in the panel. It moves to index 0, and the camera flies to face it. Returns the workspace afresh.

index.description: The form's place in the list get_workspace gives.

tools.name: take_screenshot
tools.title: Take a screenshot
tools.description: A picture of the editor's window as the player sees it now: the 3D view of the bricks and, unless `panel` is false, the settings panel down its left side. Use it to look at what has been built, since a form's brick count and discrepancy do not say how it looks. Returned as a PNG image.

max_width.description: The widest the picture may be, in pixels. 1280 if not given. A wider window is shrunk by a whole number of pixels to fit.

panel.description: False for the 3D view alone, without the panel drawn over its left side. True if not given.

tools.name: start_gif
tools.title: Start recording a GIF
tools.description: Start recording the editor's window as an animated GIF, to show a change being made or a flight of the camera. The file is written to the editor's pictures folder (Pictures/brickloft in the player's home folder) under a name with the date and time, and the answer says where. Pictures are taken at a fixed rate by the clock; while nothing in the window changes none is written, and the last one is held. Recording goes on until stop_gif, or stops by itself at 60 seconds or 64 MB. One recording at a time.

panel.description: False to record the 3D view alone, without the panel drawn over its left side. True if not given; the panel then shows in the recording, with any notice put up over the view.

size.description: How large the recording is beside the window: each of its pixels is the average of a square of 1, 2 or 3 of the window's each way. As last chosen if not given, which is half unless the player has changed it.

rate.description: Pictures a second. As last chosen if not given, which is 20 unless the player has changed it.

tools.name: stop_gif
tools.title: Stop recording the GIF
tools.description: Stop the recording started with start_gif and finish its file. The answer says where the file is, how long it plays, how many pictures it holds and how large it is, and what the recording cost the editor for each picture.

tools.name: measure_between
tools.title: Measure between two forms
tools.description: How two forms stand relative to each other: the vector and the distance from the first one's centre to the second's, in the world, and the gap between the boxes their bricks fill along each axis (a negative gap is an overlap of that much). The gap is given in the world, and also within their grid if they share one, which is the one to use for setting forms a whole number of microbricks apart.

from.description: The first form's place in the list get_workspace gives.

to.description: The second form's place in that list.

tools.name: get_camera
tools.title: Read the camera
tools.description: Where the editor's camera is in the world, in microbricks (z is up), and which way it looks: as a direction of length one, and as a heading (degrees round the upright from +x towards +y) and a tilt (degrees up from level). Also how many legs of a flight it still has to fly.

tools.name: move_camera
tools.title: Move the camera
tools.description: Send the camera along a path: to each place in turn, turning as it goes to look at that place's `look_at` point. One place moves it there; several fly it between successive coordinates, for a tour round a build. A leg with `seconds` is flown smoothly over that long, and one without is a jump. To look at a form, take its `box_in_world` from get_workspace: look at its centre from about twice its largest size away, a little above. A screenshot asked for while the camera is flying is taken when it arrives. A new path replaces one still being flown.

position.description: Where the camera goes, [x, y, z] in microbricks of the world.

look_at.description: The point it is looking at when it gets there.

seconds.description: How long the leg takes. 0 or left out: a jump.

tools.name: set_view
tools.title: Choose what is drawn
tools.description: Switch on or off what is drawn over the bricks: the rulers along each axis, the rings that turn a grid, the arrows that move it, and the dots of the form being edited. Also how far the floor is lowered below the forms, to look at one from underneath. Only what is given changes; nothing that is built is changed. Returns the settings as they now are. Switch all four off for a picture of the bricks alone, and back on afterwards: the player needs the dots to edit.

floor_below.description: How far the floor is lowered below the forms, in microbricks.

tools.name: move_point
tools.title: Move one of a form's points
tools.description: Move one of the points a form is drawn through, leaving the others where they are: an arch's foot, a centre, or one point of a spline, a Bezier curve or a revolve's profile. This is the editor's yellow dot. get_workspace lists each form's `points`, numbered from 0, measured from where the form stands. Returns the workspace afresh.

index.description: The form's place in the list get_workspace gives.

to.description: Where it goes, [x, y, z] in microbricks; a value may end in a half.

tools.name: add_pull_point
tools.title: Add a point that pulls a form out of shape
tools.description: Add a point to a form and pull the form out of shape there, as Alt + click and a drag do in the editor (the orange dot). The form moves by `pulled_by` at the place nearest `at`, and by less the further away, out to `reach`. Works on every form; a form takes up to 12. A pull within a flat curve's plane keeps it smooth; a pull out of the plane is built of sloped pieces and is rougher. Returns the workspace afresh.

index.description: The form's place in the list get_workspace gives.

at.description: A place on the form, [x, y, z] in microbricks measured as the form's points are.

pulled_by.description: How far the form moves there, [dx, dy, dz] in microbricks.

reach.description: How far from the point the form goes with it, in microbricks. This is one setting for all of a form's added points; left out, it stays as it is.

tools.name: move_pull_point
tools.title: Pull an added point further or less
tools.description: Change how far one of a form's added points pulls it. get_workspace lists each form's `added_points`, numbered from 0. Returns the workspace afresh.

index.description: The form's place in the list get_workspace gives.

pulled_by.description: How far the form now moves there, [dx, dy, dz] in microbricks from where it was before any pull.

tools.name: remove_pull_point
tools.title: Take an added point off
tools.description: Take one added point off a form, which goes back to its own shape there. The added points after it each move up one number. Returns the workspace afresh.

index.description: The form's place in the list get_workspace gives.

tools.name: line_up_arch
tools.title: Line an angled arch up with a grid of its own
tools.description: An arch whose two feet differ along both x and y stands at an angle to its grid. It then lies in no plane of the grid and is fitted cell by cell, which comes out stepped and uses many more bricks. This gives the arch a grid of its own, turned so that the arch runs straight along it, with its feet left where they are in the world; it is then fitted as smoothly as any arch. Use it after placing an arch's feet where they are wanted. The form becomes the one being edited (index 0). Returns the workspace afresh.

index.description: The form's place in the list get_workspace gives.

tools.name: list_meshes
tools.title: List the mesh files that can be built
tools.description: The mesh files in the editor's imports folder: each one's name, which is what an `imported` form's `import` setting takes (see add_form), and its size in bytes. A file gets there when the player opens it in the editor, which copies it in under a name made from its content, so the names are sixteen hexadecimal digits and `.glb`, `.obj` or `.ply`. Files anywhere else on the computer cannot be listed, opened or named through these tools.
